assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed how trade is modelled. It moved the field from industry-level to firm-level analysis, explaining export selection, reallocation and a new channel for the gains from trade. It spawned a large empirical and policy literature on trade liberalisation and productivity.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central model, and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) add the exporting-versus-FDI margin. Helpman also has a distinct earlier body of work on increasing returns and trade. Redding's contributions are substantial but more of a later extension, so I keep the proposal to two names. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made related contributions but are not credited on this ballot entry.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades since the core papers, with extensive replication, quantification and use in policy evaluation. This is mature and well confirmed.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would rather combine Helpman with Grossman (B047) or recognise firm-level trade through a different trio.
Overlap with parallel work by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum that falls outside the credited names.
Trade was recognised with Krugman in 2008, so the committee may weigh the field's recent representation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products (BLP) and the dynamic industry models of Ericson-Pakes type are the working toolkit of modern empirical industrial organisation. They underpin merger analysis, antitrust and regulatory practice, and the measurement of welfare in imperfectly competitive markets.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995) is the clearest shared contribution, and Berry (1994) is closely related. Pakes also has decades of independent work on dynamic games, patents and productivity. Bresnahan and Reiss are important to the empirical-IO foundations, but the BLP core credits the three named.
assessment.maturity: The foundations are around 30 years old. The methods are standard in academia, competition authorities and industry, so impact is very well confirmed.
uncertainties: Breadth across economics is narrower than for some macro or labour candidates.
The credit boundary with Bresnahan, Reiss and the later dynamic-games authors (Benkard, Levin) is somewhat arbitrary.
Methodological prizes depend on how the committee weighs tool-building against substantive discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work reshaped understanding of how technology and trade shocks alter labour demand, polarisation and local labour markets. The China-shock studies and the task-based approach are among the most influential empirical results of the past two decades, with large policy resonance for inequality and displaced workers.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock work. Hanson is the natural partner on the trade-exposure design. Katz has long-standing foundational contributions to skill demand, wage structure and the race between education and technology. Dorn is a key co-author of the China-shock papers but more junior, and the task-model theory also draws on Acemoglu and others outside this entry.
assessment.maturity: Roughly 15 to 25 years of cumulative evidence, with ongoing debate over long-run adjustment and magnitudes. The influence is broadly confirmed even though some quantitative conclusions are still contested.
uncertainties: Choice between Katz and Dorn for the third slot, and whether the task framework and the China shock are better treated separately.
Overlap with recent labour and technology awards (Goldin 2023, Acemoglu 2024) that touched related themes.
Debate over identification and persistence of the China-shock estimates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi showed with granular micro data that household leverage and credit supply expansions drove the housing boom and the depth of the Great Recession. This shifted both macroeconomics and financial economics toward household balance sheets and has clear policy relevance for crisis prevention and debt relief.
assessment.attribution: The core contribution is a tightly linked pair of papers and the book 'House of Debt', so the credit is unusually clean. Campbell is a major figure in asset pricing and household finance, but his contribution is different from the credit-boom work and is not essential to this discovery.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are 12 to 15 years old, which is relatively recent but sufficient for replication and wide adoption. Some of the later claims on credit-supply shocks continue to be debated.
uncertainties: Relative recency compared with candidates whose contributions are decades old.
Subsequent debate on the credit-supply versus demand interpretation and on identification of the housing boom mechanism.
The committee made a recent financial-crisis award in 2022 (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig), which may reduce room for another crisis-themed prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The credit-cycles model shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a foundational mechanism in macro-finance, widely built on in models of financial frictions and a standard reference in post-crisis macroeconomics.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is a clean two-author contribution with strong distinct identity. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial accelerator tradition, but that credit overlaps with Bernanke's earlier work and with the New Keynesian entry, so the proposal stays with the originators.
assessment.maturity: Nearly 30 years of influence and extensive use in policy models and academic work. Maturity is high.
uncertainties: Overlap with the financial accelerator line (Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist), where Bernanke has already been recognised in 2022 for related work.
Mostly a theoretical mechanism, with empirical validation arriving through later literature.
Competition for macro recognition from New Keynesian and household-debt candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This body of work measures adverse selection and moral hazard in insurance markets empirically, combining theory, structural methods and experiments (such as the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment). It informs health policy, insurance design and the welfare analysis of markets with asymmetric information.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the main drivers of the modern empirical-welfare approach, including their joint work on selection. Salanie is important for the testing of asymmetric information (with Chiappori), but the central empirical programme is carried by the first two.
assessment.maturity: The work is roughly 10 to 20 years old and has been very influential, but the youngest elements are still being tested. It is earlier in its confirmation than the older candidates.
uncertainties: Relative youth of the careers and the research programme.
Potential overlap with the earlier information-economics prize (Akerlof, Spence, Stiglitz) when assessing novelty.
How the committee would weigh the experimental evidence against the broader structural contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work established how households and villages share risk, testing full-insurance benchmarks with detailed data. It shaped development economics, social insurance design and the study of informal institutions and credit.
assessment.attribution: Townsend supplied the theoretical framework and the tests for risk sharing, together with long-run village panels such as the Thai data. Udry contributed pioneering empirical evidence from West Africa on informal insurance and intrahousehold allocation. Rosenzweig is a major development empiricist but his contribution overlaps less directly with this entry.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers are 30 years old, and later work has refined rather than overturned the main findings. Maturity is high.
uncertainties: Recent recognition of development economics in 2019 may limit space for another development award.
Mixed evidence on full risk sharing, and later debate on the interpretation of tests.
Whether Rosenzweig should be included to reflect his broader contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model is a foundational game-theoretic result with a unique subgame-perfect outcome. It underlies strategic bargaining in markets, wage setting, search and matching, and many applied models of negotiation.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is a single-author seminal result, so the credit is clear. Wolinsky (market bargaining with Rubinstein) and Binmore (related work on bargaining and the Nash programme) are significant contributors, but I propose only the originator. Stahl's concurrent contribution is a minor attribution wrinkle.
assessment.maturity: More than 40 years of confirmation and use, which gives the most mature standing on this ballot.
uncertainties: Pure theory with indirect empirical validation, and the committee may prefer applied impact.
Game theory has been recognised repeatedly (Aumann, Schelling, mechanism design, auctions), so recent field representation could weigh against it.
Whether to share the award with Wolinsky or Binmore.
